html:
Joseph Stalin was the dictator of the Soviet Union from the late 1920s until his death in 1953. He forced through collective farming and rapid industry, ran the Gulag labour camps and the Great Purge, and led the USSR to victory over Nazi Germany. Millions of his own people died in the famines, camps and killings of his rule.

He was born Ioseb Jughashvili in Gori, Georgia, the son of a shoemaker, and studied for the priesthood before turning to revolution. He joined Lenin's Bolsheviks, robbed banks for the party and spent years in Siberian exile. After 1917 he rose by controlling the party machine as General Secretary from 1922.

After Lenin died in 1924, he outmanoeuvred Trotsky and his other rivals. Then:

  • Collectivisation from 1928 forced peasants into state farms. Millions resisted, were deported or starved; the famine of 1932 to 1933 included the Holodomor in Ukraine.
  • Five-year plans built steel mills, dams and cities at great speed, using forced labour.
  • The Great Purge of 1936 to 1938 killed about 700,000 people by execution, including most of the old Bolshevik leaders and much of the army's command.

In 1939 he made a pact with Hitler and split Poland with him. Hitler invaded in 1941. The Red Army, after huge losses, won at Stalingrad and pushed on to Berlin in 1945. The Soviet Union lost some 27 million people in the war.

After the war he imposed communist governments on eastern Europe, starting the Cold War, and the Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949. He died in 1953. In 1956 his successor Khrushchev denounced his crimes. See also Muscovy, Russia, USSR.
